Methodology

Follow a rainfall upload

A feature is an input column. A target is the value the model learns to predict. For this example, the uploader chooses rainfall, measured in millimetres.

Algorithm 1 · Dictionary before LLM

For each column, look up a known synonym. If none matches, ask the locally served LLM through Ollama to infer a concept. Handle unresolved names as unknown. A new inferred concept can extend the ontology. The mapping is a dictionary from uploaded headers to concepts.

column name → known synonym? → mapped concept or LLM fallback

Algorithm 2 · Incoming edges to the target

NetworkX stores a weighted directed graph. For each uploaded attribute, map it to a node v. Keep the attribute if the graph contains an edge v → target. An edge going the other way fails this rule. Edges encode the ontology’s relationships.

selected = available columns with a mapped edge into the target
What do the orchestrator and explainable AI do?

The orchestrator coordinates execution and selection. Regression models produce the predictions. The explanation module reads intermediate metadata about the mapping, selected inputs, and model selection, then describes the recommendation in natural language.

What is the difference between a graph, an ontology, and a graph neural network?

The ontology specifies the vocabulary and relationships. The graph represents them as nodes and directed edges. This pipeline uses graph lookups to pick relevant inputs. The tree ensembles operate on the aligned table. They do not learn by sending messages along the graph.

What if the mapper gets a name wrong?

A wrong mapping can change the incoming edges queried, the features selected, and the model input alignment. A synonym match also does not prove units match. Inspect the mapping and schema, and check for target aliases before an independent evaluation.

ML foundations

How a model learns and how we measure it

Regression and decision trees

Regression predicts a number. A tree asks questions about feature values, such as whether humidity exceeds a cutoff, then returns a number at a leaf. An ensemble combines many trees.

Random Forest averages predictions from trees trained on resampled data with randomized feature choices. Boosting adds trees sequentially to improve the current predictions.

The four candidates

XGBoost uses regularized gradient boosting. CatBoost has specialized handling for categorical features. LightGBM uses histogram-based, leaf-wise tree growth. These are model characteristics. The paper compares them as candidates and does not isolate which characteristic explains a result.

The backend uses a warm-start branch for Random Forest and booster continuation for the boosting models. Think of adaptation as changing or extending an existing tree ensemble using the upload.

Move one prediction and watch the errors change

Toy data in millimetres. The last actual value is 12. Adjust its prediction. The actual median is 6, and values strictly above 6 enter the upper class.


RecordActualPredictedAbsolute errorSame median class?

What each metric measures

MAE averages absolute errors. RMSE takes the square root of the average squared errors. Squaring gives larger errors greater influence. Both are in the target’s units. R² equals 1 − (squared error of model ÷ squared error of predicting the actual mean). It is dimensionless. A negative value means the model did worse by squared error than the mean baseline on those records.

What accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC mean here

With “above the actual median” as the positive class, accuracy is the fraction of matching class labels. Precision asks how many predicted positives were actual positives, and recall asks how many actual positives were caught. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. ROC-AUC summarizes how well a score separates positives from negatives across operating thresholds. These metrics describe a binary partition. The wind result of 99.6% is partition accuracy.

Experiments

Same framework, two evaluation settings

Source pre-training

Indian Weather Repository

118,298 records. 42 raw columns and 27 selected features. Ten target-specific pipelines were pretrained. The records were randomly split with seed 42.

80% train20% test

94,638 training records and 23,660 held out. Random Forest reached R² 0.8170 on source cloud cover. This is evidence about unseen records from a random source split.

Upload adaptation

IndClim 2024–2025

7,310 daily observations from Indian cities. Four targets were evaluated. The upload supplied records for both adaptation and evaluation.

Same upload · fit and evaluate

These are in-sample measurements. Alignment can also bring in a target alias. How much any alias affected a reported score was not established.

Post-adaptation results on IndClim

TargetSelected modelR²RMSEMAEError units
HumidityLightGBM0.182916.8814.48percentage points
TemperatureLightGBM0.95571.221.02°C
PrecipitationXGBoost0.306014.798.93mm
Wind speedLightGBM0.99980.0960.07km/h

Rainfall and humidity are weak even in-sample. Temperature and wind fit the adapted records more closely. Compare errors in their own units. A larger number in millimetres versus degrees has no common interpretation.

How would we test future forecasting and the benefit of transfer?

Hold later dates aside before fitting or adapting. Keep only information available at the intended forecast time and exclude target aliases. Fit preprocessing on the training period. Compare adapted models with matched models trained from scratch on the same adaptation data and against suitable baselines. Evaluate all models on the same untouched future records. Obtain meteorologist review as a separate check of the ontology.

Model selection

Fit, agreement, and the final ranking

Knowledge Alignment Score

Put the model importance and ontology weight for each feature in the same position in two vectors. Cosine similarity measures whether the vectors point in a similar direction.

KAS = (I · W) / (‖I‖₂ × ‖W‖₂)

Toy two-feature example. The ontology gives the first feature 80% of its relative weight. Move the model’s first-feature share and see what happens.


The experiment uses cached pre-training importances. The graph is manually specified, with cached or LLM-elicited weights and a 0.5 fallback. Expert validation remains open. Hybrid feature ordering is a separate rule, Hᵢ = 0.7 Iᵢ + 0.3 Wᵢ, with heuristic weights and differently scaled inputs.

Why normalize before adding?

R² and errors have different scales and directions. Compare a metric within the same target across candidates. Min–max scaling sends the weakest value to 0 and the strongest to 1. If everyone ties, assign 1 to each.

Composite score: normalized metrics are added using the original weights. Choose the highest score within each target.

SignalMetric weightsTotal
Numerical fitR² .20 · RMSE .05 · MAE .05.30
Binary diagnosticsAccuracy .10 · F1 .10 · Precision .10 · Recall .05 · ROC-AUC .10.45
Ontology agreementKAS .25.25

The weights express a heuristic preference, and related metrics can reflect overlapping evidence. Temperature illustrates why one metric cannot tell you the ranking. LightGBM has slightly higher R², while XGBoost has slightly lower MAE.

Try the paper’s actual weight sweep

Vary the KAS weight across the nine tested settings. The other eight weights shrink or grow proportionally. Model predictions and their errors stay fixed.

Vertical axis: normalized composite score, 0–1

Why does rainfall flip?

LightGBM has higher raw rainfall KAS (0.5209 versus 0.3022), while the default composite selects XGBoost, which has stronger regression fit. Increasing the weight on normalized KAS gives LightGBM enough of an advantage at the tested weight 0.40. XGBoost still leads at 0.35. The sweep establishes the observed ranking at each tested setting.

How were the scores reconstructed?

Let k be a model’s normalized KAS. Subtract 0.25k from the saved full-precision default score to recover the eight other metrics’ combined contribution. Reweight that contribution by (1 − λ)/0.75, then add λk. This reproduces the saved score at 0.25 and avoids filling missing exported precision and recall values with zeros.

Mock examiner questions

What is novel about the study?

“The contribution is the integration of semantic schema alignment, graph-guided feature selection, adaptation of existing regressors, and knowledge-aware model ranking in one pipeline.”

Why is the wind R² so high? Can I trust it?

“It measures fit after adaptation on the same records. We would need a temporal holdout and target-alias controls to estimate future forecasting skill. Our experiment does not isolate the cause of the high fit.”

Why keep classification diagnostics in a regression study?

“They describe whether the prediction lands on the same side of a median threshold as the observation. The original composite uses them as secondary signals. R², RMSE, and MAE describe the continuous predictions directly.”

Why choose 0.25 for KAS?

“It is the original heuristic preference. We tested sensitivity by reallocating weight between KAS and the other metrics. Some selections were stable across the tested settings and rainfall changed at 0.40.”

How did the reviewer comments change the paper?

The final revision keeps the submitted framework and original scoring weights. It clarifies the 99.6% binary accuracy, foregrounds regression errors, discusses weak rainfall and humidity, qualifies KAS and its weights, fixes the sensitivity calculations, discloses in-sample evaluation and alias risk, and adds GenCast and Aurora. No new independent forecasting evaluation or expert validation was carried out.

How should I explain GenCast and Aurora in one sentence?

“GenCast addresses probabilistic medium-range weather forecasting, and Aurora is an Earth-system foundation model. Our work addresses a different problem: adapting and ranking models when tabular uploads use different schemas.”

Implementation viva · Knowledge graph and orchestrator

Trace the upload from the header to the prediction CSV. Say your answer aloud, then reveal the follow-up.

Upload handler → Map and align → Run candidates → Score and sort → Save and explain
How does the knowledge graph actually select features?

Say it aloud. “The graph is a directed NetworkX graph. A node represents a concept such as Humidity or Precipitation. The selector gets the target’s immediate incoming neighbours and checks which upload columns map to those concepts. For Precipitation, the base ontology includes incoming edges from Humidity, Temperature, Cloud, and Pressure. An edge makes the corresponding available column eligible.”

Implementation follow-up

If Cloud is absent, can the graph fill in its measured values? No. It describes a relationship. It does not create observations.

What is the difference between Rainfall, Precipitation, and precip_mm?

Say it aloud. “Rainfall is the uploaded header. Precipitation is the internal ontology concept. precip_mm is the canonical target key used by the pretrained pipeline. The slide compresses the translation to Rainfall → precip_mm. The concept in the middle is what lets differently named columns connect to the same graph node.”

Implementation follow-up

If a column is named rainfall_inches, is it now in millimetres? A semantic match alone does not convert units. Units need separate validation or conversion.

What do direction, relation labels, and weights each do?

Say it aloud. “Direction determines which target a feature points into. The relation label names the link, for example Humidity contributes_to Precipitation. The weight expresses the ontology’s assigned importance of that link. The paper’s basic selection rule checks whether an incoming edge exists. KAS uses weights when comparing profiles.”

Implementation follow-up

If A points to B and B points to C, is A automatically selected for C? No. The described lookup uses direct predecessors.

Does the knowledge graph learn from the uploaded dataset?

Say it aloud. “The base nodes and relationships are defined in the ontology. The mapper can use a local LLM as a fallback for unfamiliar headers, and the backend has an ontology expansion path. Those changes are semantic inferences. The weather regressors learn from the numeric examples during adaptation.”

Implementation follow-up

Who guarantees that the LLM inferred the correct concept or relationship? Our evaluation does not offer that guarantee. The mapping, units, and graph additions need review.

Does Algorithm 2 directly determine every input to a pretrained model?

Say it aloud. “Algorithm 2 describes eligibility by graph edges. In the pretrained backend path, alignment starts with the saved model’s required schema. It looks for an exact column match and then a concept match. The endpoint also exposes weighted graph-related features. The list of graph-related columns and the fixed model input schema can differ.”

Implementation follow-up

Why retain the fixed schema? The saved preprocessing and estimator expect those inputs. Changing the columns would require a compatible pipeline or retraining.

What happens if an expected predictor is missing or two headers map to the same concept?

Say it aloud. “The backend first tries an exact name match. If it falls back to concept matching, the reverse lookup holds one column per concept, so a later alias can overwrite an earlier one. Missing expected numeric fields can be represented as missing values for preprocessing. Missing time fields receive a default in the alignment code.”

Implementation follow-up

Why does the alias collision matter? Two headers can map to one concept yet have different units, timing, or meaning. The fallback needs explicit disambiguation and target-alias exclusion before relying on it for evaluation.

What does the orchestrator take in, and what does it return?

Say it aloud. “The upload handler has already run the candidates. It passes their result records and the target concept into choose_best_model. Each record includes measured or placeholder metrics, a feature-importance profile if available, and predictions. The function adds KAS to every record, computes each composite score against the candidate pool, sorts highest first, and returns the leading result.”

Implementation follow-up

Why compute all KAS values before any composite score? KAS is normalized across candidates. The full set of raw KAS values must exist first.

Which component actually trains the models and produces predictions?

Say it aloud. “The upload handler routes the request. Its model pipeline aligns the table, loads or trains candidates, runs predictions, and collects results. The orchestrator’s selection function receives those results and chooses the winner. The handler retrieves that candidate’s predictions, saves a CSV, and asks the explanation module to describe the choice.”

Implementation follow-up

Does the orchestrator retrain the winner after sorting? The selection function does not. In the pretrained path the handler uses the winner’s already generated predictions.

How does the backend decide whether to adapt, predict only, or train from scratch?

Say it aloud. “If a saved pipeline exists, the backend can adapt it when there are at least 20 usable numeric target values. Without the target, it runs inference only. With too few usable values, it skips adaptation. If no saved pipeline exists, scratch training requires a target column and enough valid rows.”

Implementation follow-up

What happened on IndClim? The reported adaptation ran with target labels and measured fit on the same usable records as adaptation.

How can the orchestrator select a model when the upload has no target labels?

Say it aloud. “It cannot measure fresh prediction error on that upload. In the inference-only branch, the backend gives each candidate the same placeholder numerical diagnostics. Those tied metrics contribute equally after normalization, so differences in KAS can drive the ranking.”

Implementation follow-up

Do the displayed placeholder zeros mean perfect prediction error? No. Without target labels, there is no measured error for this upload.

How does the graph turn into a KAS vector for one candidate?

Say it aloud. “Take the candidate’s feature importance keys in order. Map each feature key to a concept, look up its edge weight into the target, and put the weight at the matching position. In the backend, a feature with no corresponding ontology entry receives zero for that position. The cosine calculation compares the resulting vector with model importances.”

Implementation follow-up

Is this zero the same as the 0.5 fallback? No. Zero here represents a missing ontology match for that feature. The 0.5 fallback is used when resolving a weight for an existing relationship.

Does the generated explanation prove why a specific rainfall prediction was 12 mm?

Say it aloud. “The explanation describes the recommendation using the chosen model, available feature information, and ontology context. A statement about why the system selected a candidate is different from a local attribution for one row. Explaining a particular predicted value would require a separate per-prediction analysis.”

Implementation follow-up

Can the explanation ever change the winner? It comes after selection. The composite score has already selected the candidate.

Advanced examiner questions

Give yourself 20–30 seconds per answer. Say your answer aloud before opening the card, then try the follow-up.

Why use KAS when SHAP and permutation importance already exist?

Say it aloud. “SHAP attributes an individual prediction to its features. Permutation importance measures how much a model’s score drops when a feature is shuffled. KAS takes a model importance profile and compares it with an explicit ontology profile. I used that comparison as a model-ranking signal. An aggregated SHAP profile or held-out permutation profile could also supply the input to KAS. We didn’t test those variants.”

Examiner follow-up

How would you compare them fairly? Use a common feature set, compute each candidate’s importance by the same method on separate validation data, and compare alignment rankings and later test performance. Correlated features complicate attribution and permutation.

Why use cosine similarity instead of Spearman correlation or Euclidean distance?

Say it aloud. “Cosine compares the direction of two weight profiles. If one profile is a positive multiple of the other, their alignment is perfect. Spearman checks whether the feature order agrees, even if the relative gaps are different. Euclidean distance measures numerical distance and depends on how the profiles are scaled. Cosine suits our definition of proportional agreement. We haven’t shown it is the best choice.”

Examiner follow-up

Can two candidates share a feature ordering but have different cosine alignment? Yes. Against ontology weights [0.8, 0.2], model profiles [0.8, 0.2] and [0.55, 0.45] agree on the order, but the second allocates importance less similarly.

Is KAS just cosine similarity with a new name?

Say it aloud. “The mathematical operation is standard cosine similarity. Our contribution is defining which profiles to compare and incorporating that agreement into the workflow for ranking candidate weather models across schemas.”

Examiner follow-up

What empirical claim is defensible? We showed how including the score affects candidate selection on the recorded experiment. Its predictive value on unseen data remains open.

Can you compare feature importance across different tree libraries?

Say it aloud. “Putting the values on a common scale helps compare shares, but it doesn’t make the underlying importance definitions equivalent. The revision reports cached pre-training importance profiles. A fairer comparison would recompute the same type of importance for every adapted candidate on a common, separate validation set.”

Examiner follow-up

Would that automatically validate KAS? It would improve comparability. The ontology itself would still need independent assessment.

Did you count the ontology twice by using it in feature selection and scoring?

Say it aloud. “The graph influences two different decisions. Incoming edges determine which available features are eligible. KAS then compares relative importances among aligned features with the chosen weights. Both depend on the same ontology, so their effects are related. High agreement cannot independently validate the graph.”

Examiner follow-up

How would you isolate the effects? Compare graph selection on and off, crossed with KAS on and off, under the same held-out protocol and candidate budget. The reported weight sweep only changes the ranking rule.

Why should ontology agreement ever outweigh lower rainfall error?

Say it aloud. “It depends on what the user values. If the objective is solely lower forecast error, select with a relevant held-out error metric. Our composite also values agreement with the chosen knowledge profile. At 0.40 the ranking changes without changing either model’s predictions. That demonstrates a preference trade-off.”

Examiner follow-up

Would you deploy the 0.40 winner on this evidence? The available result is in-sample. I would first define the decision objective and compare both candidates on untouched future observations.

Why give binary metrics 45% of a score for continuous regression?

Say it aloud. “The original composite combines continuous fit, above-median classification, and ontology agreement. The binary group has a substantial influence and several of its metrics are related. The paper retains that heuristic and presents the regression results directly. A meaningful comparison would test a regression-only ranking and a regression-plus-KAS ranking under the same protocol.”

Examiner follow-up

What if the actual operational goal is severe rainfall warning? Define the event and threshold using domain needs and training data, then evaluate that objective separately. A median split does not measure severe-event performance.

Why does KAS use pre-training importance after adaptation?

Say it aloud. “The recorded pipeline reads the cached source-model profile, so the KAS in our ranking describes agreement of that profile with the ontology. Adaptation can change which inputs drive predictions. I would recompute importance after adaptation to measure that change.”

Examiner follow-up

What experiment would show whether it matters? Compare rankings from cached and recomputed profiles, then evaluate each selection on the same untouched test set.

How would you know the gain came from transfer learning rather than fitting the upload?

Say it aloud. “The before-and-after numbers alone cannot isolate the effect. I would compare a frozen pretrained model, an adapted pretrained model, and a scratch-trained model. The adapted and scratch models would use the same training period, features, and comparable tuning budgets. All three would be scored on the same later records.”

Examiner follow-up

Where do you tune the graph or ranking rule? On training or validation data. Keep the final temporal test untouched until all model-selection decisions are set.

What happens if we add a poor fifth candidate to the ranking?

Say it aloud. “The min and max are computed across the candidates. A new extreme can change a metric’s scale and therefore its effective influence on the composite. The ranking between the original candidates can shift even if their raw predictions and metrics are identical.”

Examiner follow-up

How could you test sensitivity to the candidate pool? Rerank after excluding or adding candidates. For a deployment comparison, consider normalization anchors fixed in advance on reference data.

Could near-perfect wind fit come from leakage rather than model skill?

Say it aloud. “It could be inflated by same-record evaluation or by an input that maps to the target. The experiment does not quantify either effect. I would audit feature lineage and what is available at forecast time, exclude target aliases, and compare scores on a chronological holdout.”

Examiner follow-up

Is every correlated input leakage? No. The critical questions are whether it contains target information that would be unavailable at prediction time and whether the protocol permits its use.

What if the ontology is wrong or changes between regions?

Say it aloud. “High KAS means agreement with the specified prior. If the prior is wrong or unsuitable for a region, giving it a high weight may favour a weaker model. I would ask meteorologists to review the relationships, assess agreement across expert profiles, and test the resulting selections on held-out regions or seasons.”

Examiner follow-up

Do graph weights imply causal effects? No. They encode the ontology’s assigned relationships and relative importance.
